extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, peer reviewers, and academic researchers (especially in psychology and related social sciences)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative principles for assessing journal peer-review processes, reviewer performance, and experimental studies of reviewing (e.g., tests of prestige/bias). Applies to editors designing workflows, researchers studying peer review, and reviewers concerned with reliability and ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blind reviewing of articles
rubrics_metrics.description: 'blind reviewing of articles' — the practice of concealing author identity from reviewers to reduce biases (institutional affiliation, professional status, gender).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blind review 'removes many of the biases in institutional affiliation, professional status, and gender' and is 'manifestly more fair to lesser known investigators.' Caveats: blind review can create its own problems (e.g., may lead reviewers to demand excessive methodological detail or cast doubt on authors' competence) and about one-third of manuscripts may not be truly blind. Editors should weigh fairness benefits vs practical costs and implementation details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish random error from systematic bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not confuse random evaluative error (unreliability of reviewers) with systematic bias (consistent favoritism against certain authors/institutions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peters & Ceci may have mistaken random error for bias. Use models (e.g., Stinchcombe & Ofshe) and probabilistic expectations of acceptances under assumed reliabilities to interpret resubmission outcomes before attributing effects to bias. Consider sampling error (small n) when interpreting results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interreferee reliability and validity measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use interreferee reliability coefficients and derived validity coefficients when modeling review outcomes (example: assumed interreferee reliability = .50, giving validity coefficient (sqrt of reliability) ≈ .70).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These coefficients allow estimation of probabilities that papers at different quality levels will be judged acceptable; sensitivity of expected acceptance counts to assumed reliability should be examined. Lower reliability reduces expected acceptances; reporting confidence intervals and sensitivity analyses is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental design must manipulate the independent variable to test bias
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'direct experimental test' of prestige bias requires manipulation of the independent variable (e.g., author prestige) and appropriate controls (e.g., sending equivalent numbers of manuscripts labeled as high- and low-prestige).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P&C did not manipulate prestige experimentally; better designs would include sending equivalent numbers of papers ostensibly by high- and low-status authors and using multiple article types (previously accepted, previously rejected, never submitted) so causal inference is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate sample size for inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Samples must be large enough to support statistical inference and to rule out plausible rival hypotheses; very small samples produce anecdotes rather than reliable generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study's sample of 12 (or 7 after exclusions) is too small to reject many rival hypotheses. Compute and report confidence intervals and consider power when interpreting observed differences (e.g., upper bound of 95% CI noted by Presser).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consistent measures of acceptance when computing reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing reliability (accept vs reject across times), the measures compared must be the same (e.g., original letters of acceptance/rejection vs later letters or journal appearance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P&C compared journal appearance (original measure) with later acceptance/rejection letters (later measure), which are not equivalent; reliability of dichotomous decisions requires comparable decision measures at both times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for the iterative submission–rejection–revision process
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication is often an iterative process involving rebuttal, revision, and negotiation between authors, editors, and reviewers; analyses must account for whether previous rejections were terminal or tentative and for revisions that change manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many published papers survive multiple revisions addressing reviewers' criticisms; resubmissions of final published versions may not be comparable to original submissions. Studies of review reliability or bias should consider whether rejections left open opportunities for revision and whether authors would have responded differently when re-submitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic evaluation of referees by judges, authors, and editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees should be systematically evaluated by stakeholders (judges/editors/authors) as part of improving peer review quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P&C suggested systematic evaluation of referees; commentators endorse evaluation schemes as a way to improve referee quality and accountability. Implementations might include performance records, feedback mechanisms, and periodic assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical conduct for deceptive reviewer experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Research that deceives uninformed referees/editors (e.g., submitting previously published papers under false names) raises ethical issues and requires careful cost–benefit justification, debriefing, and possibly compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One commentator called the behavior 'questionable ethical behavior' and recommended offering an honorarium for participants' professional time and thorough debriefing; stronger ethical justification is required if the research design imposes uncompensated burdens on practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use editorial boards and associate editors to screen submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ a board of associate/specialty editors to screen manuscripts for plausibility, redundancy, and fit prior to full review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JASA's practice of an initial screen by an editor and associate editor with topical interests helps detect redundancy and previously published material; journals lacking such layers may be more likely to miss resubmissions of published work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors' decisive role beyond reviewers' recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors choose which reviewers to consult and make final publication decisions; editorial judgment should mediate and weigh reviewers' recommendations rather than rely mechanically on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should not be 'editor-proof' or delegate final decisions to committee voting; a 'strong editor makes decisions that are not merely the sum of reviewers' recommendations.' Editorial pluralism among journals is protective; editors must balance adventurousness versus conservatism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications and selection of reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Select reviewers based on knowledge, experience, and desired perspective; there are trade-offs between choosing leading domain experts (may be parochial) and reviewers with modest distance who provide broader perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are not always the leading experts on a narrow problem; editors often choose reviewers who can provide perspective from a modest distance. Over-reliance on overly specialized reviewers can increase parochialism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity (signed vs anonymous reviews) — trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining reviewer anonymity can protect junior reviewers and preserve frank critique; signing reviews may reduce abusive comments but risks career consequences for junior scholars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many senior reviewers sign reviews voluntarily, but anonymity protects junior reviewers from retaliation and preserves willingness to critique senior colleagues. Editors should weigh the reduction of abuse vs loss of candidness and potential costs to reviewer pool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanically prespecified checklists as sole decision rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring reviewers and editors to 'specify exactly the criteria' for decisions risks producing mechanical checklists that favor mediocrity; final judgments are complex weighted combinations of many criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some glaring flaws can and should be specified as disqualifying, acceptance decisions often require nuanced, case-by-case weightings. Checklists can be useful for flagging clear defects but should not replace holistic editorial judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect redundancy with previously published work during screening
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and reviewers should actively detect redundancy and overlap with existing literature as part of initial screening and review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Redundancy detection can be improved using editorial boards, awareness of the journal's recent content, and cross-checking. Failure to detect redundancy contributed to the P&C resubmission findings in some journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative/usage metrics and open commentary as performance measures
rubrics_metrics.description: In electronic dissemination systems, use tallies of article accesses, commentary records, and reader feedback as additional measures of scientific performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The early PSYCH model suggested automated counting of how frequently a paper was requested and maintaining full records of comments and updated versions; such metrics can supplement CV-based measures and may encourage open peer interaction and faster dissemination. These measures can also feed into assessment of referee and article impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensate reviewers or allow opt-out for research participation
rubrics_metrics.description: When involving practicing referees/editors in research (or imposing extra workload), offer honoraria or an opt-out to respect professional time investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentators suggested that uninformed participants in deception-style research should receive honoraria and debriefing; considerations of fairness and professional norms support compensating additional time burdens.
